items.title: AMF: N1N2MessageSubscribe response timeout may orphan stored subscriptions
items.body:
### Summary

When the AMF handles an N1N2MessageSubscribe, the HTTP thread hands the work to `TASK_AMF_APP` and blocks on a future for at most `KFutureStatusTimeoutMs` (1000 ms). If the APP task does not answer within that second, the HTTP thread returns an error to the client. But the APP task, when it does run, first stores the subscription in `n1n2_message_subscribe` and only then fills the promise. A subscription that misses the deadline is therefore kept by the AMF while the client is told the request failed.

The client never receives the subscription ID (the `Location` header), so it can never call `remove_n1n2_message_subscription()`, which is keyed by that ID. The subscription is unreachable and is freed only when the whole AMF exits. Unlike the AMF/SMF PDU-session leaks, nothing overwrites it — each missed request adds a new, permanently orphaned entry.

The PoC reproduces this on a live AMF: 120 subscribe requests issued while the APP task is stalled, 120 stored, 39 answered with `201`, and 81 orphaned.


### Details

Source analysis on `v2.2.1` (April 2026), AMF commit `513c0f2`.

**1. The HTTP thread waits one second, then gives up**

https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/513c0f2dc4175e7d8f099a41d4a797913d3cf40e/src/sbi/amf_http2_server.cpp#L1132-L1150

The handler creates a promise, sends `itti_sbi_n1n2_message_subscribe` to `TASK_AMF_APP`, and calls `wait_for_result(f, result_opt)`. That helper waits a single `KFutureStatusTimeoutMs` and returns `nullopt` on timeout (`oai-cn5g-common-src`, `utils/utils.hpp:18,32-46`). On `nullopt` the handler responds with an error and stops waiting.

**2. The APP task stores the subscription before it answers**

https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/513c0f2dc4175e7d8f099a41d4a797913d3cf40e/src/amf-app/amf_app.cpp#L862-L890

`add_n1n2_message_subscription()` (`:870`) inserts into the map first; `trigger_process_response()` (`:889`) fills the promise last. If the HTTP thread has already timed out, the insert has still happened and the promise-fill has no one listening.

https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/513c0f2dc4175e7d8f099a41d4a797913d3cf40e/src/amf-app/amf_app.cpp#L2119-L2127

**3. Cleanup needs the ID the client never got**

https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/513c0f2dc4175e7d8f099a41d4a797913d3cf40e/src/amf-app/amf_app.cpp#L2130-L2139

`remove_n1n2_message_subscription()` erases by `(ue_ctx_id, sub_id)`. The subscription ID is returned to the client only in the `201` `Location` header, which a timed-out request never sends. With no ID, the client cannot unsubscribe, and no other path removes the entry.

**What makes the APP task miss the deadline.** `TASK_AMF_APP` is single-threaded. Any handler that blocks it for ≥1 s pushes queued subscribe requests past their own timeout. One such path exists in-tree: `get_nrfs()` (`amf_app.cpp:2623`), reached from `update_amf_configuration` → `register_to_nrf()`, waits on an NSSF response per configured slice when `enable_nssf` is set. If the NSSF does not answer, each wait runs the full `KFutureStatusTimeoutMs`. Other operational causes — CPU-constrained node, scheduling pressure — produce the same effect without any specific code path.

### PoC

On `oai-amf:v2.2.1`, no source change.

**How the AMF is made to miss the deadline.** A subscribe only leaks if `TASK_AMF_APP` is busy when it arrives. `enable_nssf` is turned on and a fake `oai-nssf` is placed on the network that accepts TCP connections but never sends a reply. An AMF configuration `PUT` reaches `get_nrfs()`, which waits on that NSSF and runs the full 1000 ms timeout. Measured: the `PUT` returns `504` after `1.038 s`, and the AMF log shows the NSSF request at `02:38:20.061` with the next inbound request at `02:38:21.062` and nothing in between — the task really is stalled for that second.

**What is sent.** Three identical cycles. In each, the configuration `PUT` is looped to keep the task stalled, and 40 N1N2MessageSubscribe requests are sent at 0.1 s intervals for the same UE. Nothing is ever unsubscribed.

**What is counted.** On the client, the HTTP status of each of the 40 requests. On the AMF, the map size as (`Add an N1N2 Message Subscribe`) minus (`Remove an N1N2 Message Subscribe`) in the log. The two are counted separately so the AMF's view and the client's view can be compared.

```
                  map size | sent | 201 | 504 (timed out)
start                    0 |      |     |
after cycle 1           40 |   40 |  13 |  27
after cycle 2           80 |   40 |  13 |  27
after cycle 3          120 |   40 |  13 |  27
after 30 s idle        120 |      |     |

total: 120 sent, 39 x 201, 81 x 504, 0 removals logged
```

**The leak.** All 40 requests per cycle land in the map, but only 13 of them got a `201`. The other 27 got a `504`: the HTTP thread had already given up, so no `Location` header was sent and the client holds no subscription ID. The AMF kept them anyway — the insert happens before the promise is filled. Over three cycles that is 81 entries the AMF stores and the client cannot name. Since `remove_n1n2_message_subscription()` takes only that ID, nothing can ever delete them, which is why the removal count stays at 0.

**The accumulation.** The map rises by exactly 40 each cycle, never less. Subscription IDs are generated fresh per request, so a repeat subscribe for the same UE creates a new entry instead of replacing the old one — retrying does not clean up. And the count is unchanged 30 s later, so there is no expiry either. The only bound is the lifetime of the AMF process.

### Impact

The subscription stays in `n1n2_message_subscribe` for the life of the AMF process. The client believes the request failed and holds no ID, so `remove_n1n2_message_subscription()` can never target it; the AMF/SMF PDU-session leaks are at least overwritten on retry, but here each missed request adds a fresh, permanent entry.

Reaching the timeout needs the APP task blocked for a second. The clearest in-tree trigger is `get_nrfs()` waiting on an unresponsive NSSF, which requires `enable_nssf` and a reconfiguration; more generally, a CPU-constrained or overloaded AMF reaches the same window without any special path. Whenever that window overlaps NF subscribe traffic, orphaned subscriptions accumulate.

The growth is not bounded by an identity space the way the PDU-session maps are: subscription IDs are freshly generated per request, so the map grows with the number of timed-out subscribes over the AMF's lifetime.

items.title: AMF accepts registration updates but rejects valid Registration Complete
items.body:
## Summary

OAI AMF v2.2.2 accepts a registration update while its mobility-management state remains DEREGISTERED, then rejects the corresponding Registration Complete with cause 101. The Complete passes NAS integrity verification. The same update path also accepts a plaintext SHT=0 request using an existing security context, with integrity verification of the triggering request and authentication recovery omitted.

The starting condition is an initial Registration Accept containing a GUTI whose confirmation is still pending. The UE has entered REGISTERED locally, while the AMF is waiting for Registration Complete. A Service Reject with cause 101 changes the AMF to DEREGISTERED; the UE continues in REGISTERED with its existing GUTI and NAS security context. A subsequent registration update receives another Accept, followed by rejection of its valid Complete.

This produces two connected failures: an unprotected request drives registration-update processing, and an accepted update has a broken completion path.

## Triggering path and observed results

Execute the following NAS input sequence from a fresh core/gNB/UE session. Send the Service Request while confirmation of the first Registration Accept is still pending.

```text
registrationRequest
→ authenticationResponse
→ securityModeComplete
→ serviceRequest
→ registrationRequest (configuration under test)
```

The observed responses are:

```text
authenticationRequest
→ securityModeCommand
→ registrationAccept
→ serviceReject (cause 101)
→ registrationAccept
```

The last input is a Registration Request with the identity, registration type and security header selected from the table below. The harness command for the GUTI identity is `registrationRequestGUTI`.

| Identity     | Registration type  | Uplink SHT | Target response     |
| ------------ | ------------------ | ---------- | ------------------- |
| SUCI or GUTI | 2: mobility update | 0, 1, 2    | Registration Accept |
| SUCI or GUTI | 3: periodic update | 1          | Registration Accept |

Every listed variant receives an Accept with outer SHT=2. Sending `registrationComplete` immediately afterwards produces `registrationReject` with cause 101. The AMF remains DEREGISTERED, and the Complete passes NAS integrity verification.

The representative GUTI/type2/SHT0 and SHT1 cases exercise connection release and re-establishment before the target request. The connection's 5G-S-TMSI identifies the existing AMF/NAS context.

For SHT=0, the AMF proceeds directly to the update Accept using the existing keys, skipping current-request integrity verification, a new authentication procedure, and security-mode recovery. For SHT=1, both the request and its Complete pass integrity verification, and the AMF still rejects completion because its state is DEREGISTERED.

An initial-registration control (type 1) instead receives Authentication Request at the target step, enters authentication and security-mode control, completes registration, and subsequently receives Service Accept.

[public-evidence.zip](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/33621595/public-evidence.zip)

## Source analysis

The following references use AMF commit `b2f19d1a4a6f23471f218316b33adc61505035f7`.

1. **The context survives connection release.** The N2 release-complete handler removes the NGAP association while keeping the AMF/NAS context available for the next connection: [amf_n2.cpp, lines 1762–1770](https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/b2f19d1a4a6f23471f218316b33adc61505035f7/src/amf-app/amf_n2.cpp#L1762-L1770).
2. **Service Reject changes the AMF state.** `service_request_handle()` returns cause 101 for the pending-registration state. `send_service_reject(nc, cause)` dispatches `SERVICE_REJECT_SENT`, moving the AMF to DEREGISTERED while the security context remains available: [amf_n1.cpp, lines 1415–1426](https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/b2f19d1a4a6f23471f218316b33adc61505035f7/src/amf-app/amf_n1.cpp#L1415-L1426), [lines 1883–1887](https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/b2f19d1a4a6f23471f218316b33adc61505035f7/src/amf-app/amf_n1.cpp#L1883-L1887).
3. **The update handler checks a transition but leaves it uncommitted.** `run_mobility_registration_update_procedure()` calls `check_nas_event(REGISTRATION_REQUEST_RECEIVED)`, then uses the presence of `security_ctx` to select the direct-Accept path. It creates an Accept containing a GUTI while omitting the associated state transition and T3550 setup: [amf_n1.cpp, lines 5036–5239](https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/b2f19d1a4a6f23471f218316b33adc61505035f7/src/amf-app/amf_n1.cpp#L5036-L5239). `check_nas_event()` validates a possible transition; state mutation belongs to the event-handling path: [nas_state_machine.cpp, lines 282–296](https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/b2f19d1a4a6f23471f218316b33adc61505035f7/src/amf-app/nas_state_machine.cpp#L282-L296). The periodic-update handlers have the same omission.
4. **The plaintext-request path reaches the same acceptance decision.** SHT=0 Registration Request passes the plaintext allowlist. The update handler bases acceptance on the existing security-context object rather than successful authentication of this request: [amf_n1.cpp, lines 479–590](https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/b2f19d1a4a6f23471f218316b33adc61505035f7/src/amf-app/amf_n1.cpp#L479-L590), [lines 5060–5076](https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/b2f19d1a4a6f23471f218316b33adc61505035f7/src/amf-app/amf_n1.cpp#L5060-L5076).
5. **Complete reaches the stale state.** `registration_complete_handle()` sees DEREGISTERED and returns cause 101. The code that stops T3550 and commits registration completion lies after this failed state check: [amf_n1.cpp, lines 4109–4151](https://github.com/openairinterface/oai-cn5g-amf/blob/b2f19d1a4a6f23471f218316b33adc61505035f7/src/amf-app/amf_n1.cpp#L4109-L4151).

The resulting inconsistency is between the acceptance decision, request authentication, and the AMF state required to complete the accepted procedure.

## Expected behavior and security significance

[TS 24.501 §5.5.1.3.4](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/124500_124599/124501/17.10.01_60/ts_124501v171001p.pdf#page=340) requires the AMF to start T3550 and enter COMMON-PROCEDURE-INITIATED when an update Accept contains a GUTI. On the corresponding Complete, the AMF stops T3550 and enters REGISTERED. The observed DEREGISTERED → Accept → rejected Complete behavior violates this required progression.

[TS 33.501 §6.4.6](https://www.etsi.org/deliver/etsi_ts/133500_133599/133501/17.10.00_60/ts_133501v171000p.pdf#page=67) defines authentication and security establishment for initial NAS messages. Existing keys identify an available security context; verification of the current request establishes its authenticity. The SHT=0 case skips that distinction and allows an unprotected request to drive update processing and a protected response. Encrypting and authenticating the response protects the response itself; the triggering request still requires authentication.

For SHT=0, the AMF processes the update using an existing context while skipping current-request integrity verification and a new authentication procedure. The state-management impact is rejection of a valid completion message after the AMF has accepted the update, disrupting registration recovery.

## Affected version and evidence

- AMF: v2.2.2, commit `b2f19d1a4a6f23471f218316b33adc61505035f7`.
- common-src: `c0dcc9aa70da170b3dcd690a34e704be4199f3fd`.
- Deployment: official-revision AMF build, image `oai-amf:upstream-v2.2.2`; companion core NFs v2.2.1.
- Test client: modified UERANSIM v3.2.6 with explicit NAS input control.
- Environment: Ubuntu 22.04.5 LTS, kernel 6.8.0-138-generic, 4 virtual CPUs on AMD Ryzen 7 9700X, approximately 7.7 GiB RAM and 38.7 GiB disk; Docker 29.6.2 and Compose v5.3.1.

`public-evidence.zip` contains the triggering path, tested configurations, representative decoded fields, short AMF event excerpts, source references, and version information. Test-harness commands and full selected NAS traces are prepared in `maintainer-details.zip` for maintainer follow-up.

items.title: [Bug]: `uint16_t` Truncation in `Type6NasIe::Validate()` Defeats the Only Length Check on Every Type 6 NAS IE
items.body:
### Description

A pre-authentication denial-of-service vulnerability exists in the OAI CN5G AMF NAS decoder. `Type6NasIe::Validate()` is the **single** upper-bound length check applied to every Type 6 NAS information element before its content decoder runs; it compares the remaining buffer length against the IE length, but stores that length — which `GetIeLength()` correctly computes as a `uint32_t` — into a local declared as **`uint16_t`**. A malformed **5GS Mobile Identity IE** of type IMEISV declaring a length indicator `li_ = 65535` computes `GetIeLength() = 2 + 65535 = 65537`, which truncates to **1**, so the comparison becomes `23 < 1` — false — and the guard is completely defeated. The declared length then reaches `_5gsMobileIdentity::DecodeImeisv()`, the one identity branch that is never told the real buffer size, whose unbounded loop walks **65535 octets out of a 27-octet NAS heap buffer** (CWE-125). By sending crafted NAS Registration Requests through NGAP/SCTP, a rogue gNB can crash the AMF process (SIGSEGV, exit 139) — reproduced **3/3** across independent from-scratch deployments.

When the walk happens to stay inside mapped memory, the decode *completes* and the AMF renders the out-of-bounds heap bytes as decimal digits into its own log — up to **137,387 characters in a single line** observed (CWE-200; log-local in this version, see *Impact*).

The vulnerability is reachable before authentication and does not require:
- A valid SIM card
- A provisioned subscriber
- NAS security context
- Successful authentication

### Affected Component

Tested Image: `oaisoftwarealliance/oai-amf:v2.2.1`

The defect lives in the shared NAS library (`src/common-src`), so it is compiled into **every AMF build from this source tree**, and **14 IE classes** derive from `Type6NasIe`, all inheriting the same truncated `Validate()` (IMEISV is simply the branch where the missing bound is directly exploitable).

Affected code path:
```
RegistrationRequest::Decode
        |
        |_Type6NasIe::Decode
                |
                Type6NasIe::Validate()      <- uint16_t truncation bypass
                        |
                        _5gsMobileIdentity::Decode
                                |
                                DecodeImeisv()           <- unbounded loop, OOB read
```

### Root Cause

The vulnerability is caused by a `uint32_t -> uint16_t` narrowing in the only length gate of a Type 6 NAS IE (`src/common-src/nas/ies/Type6NasIe.cpp:59`):

```cpp
bool Type6NasIe::Validate(int len) const {
  uint16_t ie_len = GetIeLength();   // GetIeLength() returns uint32_t: 2 + 65535 = 65537 -> 1
  if (len < ie_len) { ...; return false; }
}
```

`GetIeLength()` deliberately returns `uint32_t` precisely because `GetHeaderLength() + li_` can exceed `UINT16_MAX`; the caller then throws that width away. For a 2-octet header (`is_iei == false` in `RegistrationRequest.cpp:835`):

```
li_ (wire)   GetIeLength() (uint32_t)   uint16_t ie_len   Validate (23-octet remainder)
65533        65535                      65535             REJECTED  <-- safe control
65534        65536                      0                 ACCEPTED  <-- bypass
65535        65537                      1                 ACCEPTED  <-- bypass (default attack)
```

The check is **inverted by the truncation**: declaring *more* data makes the IE *more* likely to pass. `_5gsMobileIdentity::Decode()` then recovers the true `li_` via `GetLengthIndicator()` — the full 65535, not the truncated local — and dispatches on the type-of-identity nibble:

```cpp
switch (octet & 0x07) {
  case kSuci:    DecodeSuci(buf + decoded_size, len - decoded_size, ie_len);  // real buffer
  case k5gGuti:  Decode5gGuti(buf + decoded_size, len - decoded_size);        // real buffer
  case k5gSTmsi: Decode5gSTmsi(buf + decoded_size, len - decoded_size);       // real buffer
  case kImeisv:  DecodeImeisv(buf + decoded_size, ie_len);                    // NO buffer bound
}
```

Three of the four identity branches receive the real remaining buffer size; the IMEISV branch alone is handed only the attacker-declared length. `DecodeImeisv()` then runs an unbounded loop with the unchecked `DECODE_U8` macro — a bare dereference; the codebase's own bounds-checked variant `DECODE_U8_VALUE` already guards the option-IEI walk immediately after the mobile identity (`RegistrationRequest.cpp:842`):

```cpp
for (int i = 0; i < len; i++) {                        // len == 65535, NO buffer bound
  DECODE_U8(buf + decoded_size, octet, decoded_size);
```

`Type6NasIe.cpp:59` is the **only site in the entire NAS library** that narrows `GetIeLength()` to `uint16_t`; three sibling decoders (`EapMessage.cpp:89`, `UeRadioCapabilityId.cpp:85`, `ExtendedProtocolConfigurationOptions.cpp:174`) already compare against the untruncated `uint32_t` and correctly reject `li_ = 65535` — the fix pattern is established in-repo and needs no design decision.

### Reproduction
[POC](https://github.com/hackeryounow/5GCVulDB/tree/main/CVE-2026-117069)
```sh
go build -o imeisv_oob .
docker inspect oai-amf \
  --format '{{range .NetworkSettings.Networks}}{{.IPAddress}}{{end}}'   # -> AMF NGAP IP
./imeisv_oob \
    --host <AMF_NGAP_IP> \
    --port 38412 \
    --li 65535 \
    --repeat 2000
# Wait a minute
docker inspect oai-amf \
  --format '{{.State.Status}} ExitCode={{.State.ExitCode}}'
# Output:
# exited ExitCode=139
```

The PoC is a rogue gNB: one SCTP association to N2 port 38412, an unauthenticated `NGSetupRequest` (the AMF does not authenticate gNBs), then `InitialUEMessage`s carrying the 27-octet crafted Registration Request (69-octet NGAP PDU on the wire). Across three independent from-scratch deployments the AMF crashed after **16 / 38 / 20** requests (3/3), always at the same instruction — `DecodeImeisv+610`, the inlined `DECODE_U8` byte load, fault offset `0x14ad812` identical in all three runs — with `dmesg` recording `error 4` (user-mode read of a non-present page) inside `oai_amf` itself.

The last three AMF log lines are the fingerprint of the bug:

```
[nas] [debug] Decoding 5GSMobilityIdentity
[nas] [debug] Decoded 5GSMobilityIdentity IE length 65535     <- Validate() accepted a 65535-octet IE in a 27-octet message
[nas] [debug] Decoding 5GSMobilityIdentity IMEISV              <- last line before SIGSEGV
```

Safe control: `--li 65533` (two below the attack value) does not wrap — `GetIeLength() = 65535` fits in `uint16_t`, `Validate()` rejects the IE at `Type6NasIe.cpp:128` before any dispatch, and the AMF survived **2000** such requests in all three runs (3/3). This differential proves the crash is caused by the truncation, not by malformed NAS in general.

### Impact

An attacker capable of sending NGAP messages to the AMF can repeatedly send crafted Registration Requests and terminate the AMF process — one unauthenticated packet class, replayable at will, against the N1/N2 control-plane anchor of the 5G core.
- AMF control-plane service unavailable: every attached gNB loses its NGAP association and its AMF context
- Existing UE registrations are interrupted: no registration, paging, handover or service request; PDU session establishment fails after five retransmissions
- The AMF stops its periodic NRF profile updates, so its registration goes stale and it can no longer be discovered by other NFs
- No restart policy in the default deployment: the container stays down (`exit=139`, `restarts=0`) until a manual restart
- Secondary: when the walk stays inside mapped memory, up to ~137 KB of AMF heap is rendered into the AMF log per request (observed 137,387 characters) — a CWE-200 exposure to the log sink and a log-flooding / disk-exhaustion vector whose volume is attacker-controlled. In v2.2.1 the decoded IMEISV never reaches the SBI `pei` field (hardcoded at `amf_sbi.cpp:727`), so no remote exfiltration is claimed; should that placeholder ever be fixed to use the real PEI, the same bug becomes a remote heap-disclosure primitive over SBI with no further change.

### Weaknesses
- CWE-197: Numeric Truncation Error (root cause)
- CWE-125: Out-of-bounds Read
- CWE-200: Exposure of Sensitive Information to an Unauthorized Actor (secondary, log-local)
- CWE-306: Missing Authentication for Critical Function (contributing — N2 does not authenticate gNBs)
